**Sources (abbreviations used below)**
- [EW] https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-6/
- [EW-es] https://es.enduringword.com/comentario-biblico/job-6/ (the Spanish edition, which kept some quotes the English excerpt cut off)
- [EBC] https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/teb/job-6.html (the 1887 Expositor's Bible, edited by Nicoll)
- [SL6] https://www.studylight.org/commentary/job/6-6.html (excerpts from Coffman, Constable, the Preacher's Complete Homiletical Commentary and the Biblical Illustrator)
- [PC] https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/job-6.html (Pulpit Commentary)

---

**1. The traditional reading**

**v. 1:** The friends sat silently with Job for seven days (2:13). Job then cried out (ch. 3), Eliphaz called him to repent (chs. 4–5), and now Job answers. [EW]
- Coffman finds Job's words strong and clear, compared with Eliphaz's wandering speech that lacks clear conviction. [SL6]

**vv. 2–3:** Eliphaz's well-meant but wrong diagnosis made Job's suffering worse. Guzik ties this to God's verdict in 42:7 that the friends did not speak rightly about Him. [EW]
- Job admits his words in ch. 3 were rash. They didn't curse God but came close, and he blames the crushing weight of his grief. Morgan's point: Eliphaz didn't understand the cry because he didn't know the pain. [EW]
- Constable says Job's calamities were heavy like wet sand. He also says one Hebrew word in this opening section occurs nowhere else in the Old Testament. His note calls it "iniquity" in 6:2, which doesn't match the BSB wording, so check that before you use it. [SL6]

**v. 4:** Job feels that God Himself has attacked him with arrows, poison and terrors. [EW]
- Guzik quotes an unnamed commentator who reads this as poisoned arrows causing a burning fever and terrible thirst. [EW]
- The arrows-and-poison picture marks God as Job's attacker in this speech. [EW]
- The Biblical Illustrator contrasts Job with a martyr. A martyr is held up by the cause he dies for, but Job has no explanation. The God he thought he was at peace with now seems an angry, baffling power, and crying out is the last thing he can do. [SL6]

**v. 5:** A donkey or ox doesn't cry out when it has food. In the same way, Job isn't complaining without reason. [EW]
- If Eliphaz's words had satisfied him, he wouldn't have cried out as he did. [EW]

**v. 6:** Job is describing how Eliphaz's words "tasted": bland, with nothing to strengthen him. [EW]
- Guzik quotes Spurgeon: Eliphaz's speech had no sweetness because it had no sympathy or comfort. [EW]
- On the Job 1 page, Guzik quotes a writer who says scholars still don't know what substance the phrase rendered "white of an egg" refers to, though Job's disgust is plain. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-1/

**v. 7:** Eliphaz's words were like rotten, disgusting food. This food imagery runs through the whole chapter and comes back in v. 30. [EW], [EW-es]

**vv. 8–9:** Job returns to his wish from ch. 3 to be dead. He never seems to consider suicide; he wants God to end his life. "Unleash His hand" may again picture God as an archer firing the final arrow. [EW]
- Morgan: when the answer doesn't come and the pain goes on, we should trust there is an explanation, and that one day we will thank God for not granting our request. [EW-es]
- The Pulpit Commentary says the destruction Eliphaz had threatened Job with is exactly what Job now longs for. [PC]

**v. 10:** Job insists he is basically innocent before God. Guzik prefers "not denied" (NIV) to "not concealed."
- Smick: Job's one remaining comfort was that he hadn't denied God's words, even while he firmly rejected Eliphaz's. [EW]
- The Spanish edition adds an application: we have an even greater duty than Job not to hide God's words. [EW-es]
- Expositor's Bible: with a clear conscience, Job isn't afraid to die. He wants to die while still faithful, because if he lived on, weakened and sick, he couldn't be sure of himself. It calls this passage remarkably daring piety and says a person may speak frankly to God, as long as they are fully in earnest. [EBC]

**vv. 11–12:** Job speaks with the hopelessness of someone in severe, ongoing pain who has no strength left for what is coming. [EW]
- The Pulpit Commentary renders the end of v. 11 as "that I should stretch out my spirit." Job can't hope for the happy ending Eliphaz promised, so he can't make himself wait patiently. [PC]
- The Preacher's Complete Homiletical Commentary reads "hope" as hope of recovering the earthly blessings Eliphaz held out, and "end" as the end of his miseries. [SL6]
- Homilies in the Pulpit Commentary (by Green and Johnson) see here a confession of complete weakness. If death must come, why not sooner? [PC]

**v. 13:** This is not self-help talk about looking inward. Job is saying he is completely helpless. If his only help is inside himself, he has none. Guzik recommends the NIV wording. [EW]
- Smick: Job's words can comfort sufferers who have felt rage but were too ashamed to say so. [EW-es]

**v. 14:** This is Job's central charge. His friends should show kindness even if he *had* given up the fear of God. [EW]
- Adeney's homily: a friend gives strength to endure. Bearing one another's burdens keeps a soul from despair. [PC]

**vv. 15–17:** Only Eliphaz has spoken, but Job addresses all his "brothers." He may be being polite, or he may take the others' silence as agreement. They are as unreliable as a snow-fed stream that disappears in the heat. [EW], [EW-es]
- Andersen: the snow imagery suggests Job's homeland was east of the Lebanon ranges rather than near Edom. [EW-es]

**vv. 18–20:** None of the pages I read discuss these verses individually; they are covered under the brook image above.

**v. 21:** Guzik calls this the climax of Job's response. He quotes a writer who sees it as a sermon on the courage it takes to stay with people in dreadful condition, because the risk makes us afraid. [EW]

**vv. 22–23:** Job wasn't asking for money or a rescue from raiders. He only wanted comfort, and he got none. [EW-es]

**vv. 24–25:** "Teach me," "help me understand" and "what does your argument prove?" are all demands for evidence.
- Lawson: Eliphaz blames sin but never names one, so until he does, his argument proves nothing. [EW]

**v. 26:** Eliphaz was too harsh and didn't see that ch. 3 was the speech of a desperate man.
- Mason: the friends hint, moralize and hedge but never identify a real problem. The best they can do is criticize his "attitude." [EW]

**v. 27:** Andersen sees Job hitting back with his own charges. There is no more evidence that the friends gambled over orphans than that Job asked for bribes; the friendship has turned into trading insults. [EW]

**v. 28:** Mason pictures the friends with their heads down, refusing to meet Job's eyes, while the sick man holds his head up. [EW-es]

**v. 29:** Job wants them to admit that his suffering is not punishment for some hidden sin. [EW]
- The Preacher's Complete Homiletical Commentary has a heading saying Job renounces all righteousness but Christ's before God, while carefully keeping his reputation spotless before men. The excerpt didn't show which verse it belongs to. It probably relates to "my righteousness," but check before you use it. [SL6]

**v. 30:** This closes the food imagery. Job's "taste" can tell that Eliphaz's words are unsavory. [EW]

---

To fill the gaps, I'd suggest a fresh session: Ellicott, Gill and Barnes on Biblehub, Precept Austin, the NET Bible notes on vv. 6, 10 and 14, and the tradition-specific and Catholic/Orthodox sites.
